summary: Govind Sadashiv Ghurye worked in Indology and related fields. He studied at Bahauddin College, Elphinstone College, and the University of Cambridge under W. H. R. Rivers and Alfred Cort Haddon. He later headed the University of Mumbai's Sociology Department (1924–1959).

Govind Swamirao Gai specialized in Indology, history, archaeology, and linguistics. He served as Chief Epigraphist for the Government of India (attested 1958–1967) and the Archaeological Survey of India (1966–1976), and as an epigraphy consultant for the American Institute of Indian Studies in 1986.

Govind Vinayak Devasthali was an Indology scholar who studied under Hari Damodar Velankar. He served as Professor of Sanskrit at HPT Arts & RYK Science College (attested 1944) and Professor at Savitribai Phule Pune University (attested 1967–1968).

Govindlal Hargovind Bhatt worked in Indology. He served as a professor at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda (attested 1933–1939) and later as Director of the Oriental Institute, Vadodara (attested 1953–1957).
Grace Constant Lounsbery worked in Buddhist studies. She studied at Bryn Mawr College and served as president of Les Amis du Bouddhisme, an organization she founded in 1929, from circa 1929 to 1964.

Grace Morley was an archaeologist, historian, and Indologist educated at UC Berkeley and the University of Paris. She directed the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1934–1958), the National Museum, New Delhi (1960–1966), and headed the International Council of Museums (1967–1978).

Grace S. Fong is a Sinologist who studied at McGill University and the University of British Columbia. She held a professorship at Smith College (circa 1985–1989) and chaired the Department of East Asian Studies as associate professor at McGill around 1989.
Grace Sturtevant Hopkins was a linguist who graduated from Vassar College and earned her Ph.D. at Yale University, where she studied under Edgar Howard Sturtevant from circa 1927 to 1932.

Graeme MacQueen was a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. He completed his doctoral studies at Harvard University under Masatoshi Nagatomi and served as a lecturer at McMaster University from circa 1977 to 2003.

Grafton Elliot Smith worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Sydney Medical School, the University of Sydney, and St John's College, and held a post at University College London from circa 1919 to 1936.
Graham E. Clarke worked in Tibetology and other fields. He held posts at the Institute of Development Studies and at the University of Oxford, where he was attested as a Senior Member in 1998.
Graham Lock is a scholar in Buddhist studies and linguistics who studied under Hsuan Hua and Saddhaloka Bhikkhu.

Graham M. Schweig is an Indology, religious studies, and philosophy scholar. Attested in 2021, he held posts at Christopher Newport University, the Graduate Theological Union, and as Director of Theology at Avanti Schools Trust.

Graham Parkes is a scholar of philosophy and Japanology who earned his Ph.D. at UC Berkeley. He served as Professor of Philosophy at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (1991–2008) and later held professorial and leadership roles at University College Cork (2008–2013).

Graham Priest is a philosopher and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at St John's College, Cambridge, and completed his Ph.D. under John Lane Bell at LSE. His appointments include Boyce Gibson Professor at Melbourne and Distinguished Professor at CUNY Graduate Center.
Graham Sandberg was a scholar in Tibetology and linguistics. He studied at Trinity College Dublin and the Inner Temple, and later served as a chaplain for the Government of India from 1885 to 1904.

Grant Parker is a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He earned his MA at the University of Cape Town and his PhD at Princeton University, later teaching at Duke University (1999–2006) and Stanford University (appointed 2006).

Graves Champney Haughton was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Fort William College. He served as Assistant Professor (1817) and Professor of Hindú Literature and the History of Asia (1819–1827) at the East India Company College.

Gray Tuttle is a scholar of Tibetology, Sinology, and history. He studied at Princeton and Harvard, working with Nicola Di Cosmo, William Kirby, Leonard van der Kuijp, and Philip Kuhn, and was appointed Associate Professor at Columbia University in 2005.
Graziadio Isaia Ascoli was a linguist and Indologist who was tutored by Samuel David Luzzatto. He served as a professor at the Accademia Scientifico-Letteraria di Milano from 1861 to 1902.
